question: First live instantiation of the selector-study protocol: on real noisy ALFWorld episodes at the headroom-respecting panel size (validation 8), does a noise-band arm differ from the strict control gate, and what does the double-scoring accounting show?

design.grid: reduced pilot: one seed, two arms, two attempts (the protocol's full 3x3 grid remains the definitive study)

arms.selector: noise_band 0.13 (the measured one-game swing on 8-game validation)

design.rationale: the 2026-10-18 pilot was stopped by the protocol's headroom precondition at validation 4; this redesign keeps one game of headroom (baseline 0.875 on both arms)

verdict: DEGENERATE COMPARISON, HONESTLY NULL: no proposal cleared even the strict gate on either arm (all ties at 0.875), so the noise band never bound - zero false-blocks because there was nothing to block. The binding constraint at this scale is proposal quality, not gate noise sensitivity. The cross-arm final panels differ by up to two games with identical initial skills, reproducing the known single-draw noise. The pilot's value is machinery: the protocol ran live end-to-end (headroom check, two arms, lifecycle, freeze/final, verify, double-scoring accounting) and the full 3-seed study now has a costed, working template.
limits: One seed, two attempts, flash tier, single final repeat per condition. A degenerate selector comparison cannot inform selector design; it does establish that at this proposer tier and panel, gaining acceptance at all is the hard step. Next live study needs more attempts, a stronger proposer, or tasks where single edits move multiple games.
